answers.brief_reasoning: By the quotient rule, f'(x) = A(B − x²)/(x² + B)². Setting f'(1) = 0 gives B = 1. Then f(1) = A/2 = 1, so A = 2.
The denominator has a higher degree than the numerator, so f(x) goes to 0 as x goes to positive or negative infinity.
answers.final_answer: Both limits equal 0. The horizontal asymptote is y = 0.

answers.brief_reasoning: f'(x) = 2(1 − x²)/(x² + 1)². So f' < 0 for x < −1, f' > 0 for −1 < x < 1, and f' < 0 for x > 1. This gives a relative minimum f(−1) = −1 and a relative maximum f(1) = 1. f is continuous everywhere, these are its only critical points, and f(x) goes to 0 at both ends. So 1 is the absolute maximum and −1 is the absolute minimum. A direct check: 1 − f(x) = (x − 1)²/(x² + 1) ≥ 0 and f(x) + 1 = (x + 1)²/(x² + 1) ≥ 0.
answers.final_answer: The absolute maximum is 1, at x = 1. The absolute minimum is −1, at x = −1.

answers.brief_reasoning: f(x) = k is the same as kx² − 2x + k = 0. If k = 0, the only solution is x = 0. If k ≠ 0, the equation is quadratic with discriminant 4 − 4k². It has two distinct real roots exactly when |k| < 1. When |k| = 1 there is one root, and when |k| > 1 there are none. This matches the shape of f: it rises from 0 down to −1, climbs to 1, then falls back toward 0.
